## The Wish {.center}

Real data is messy: fat-tailed, curved, dependent.

. . .

**A Gaussian is the opposite** — every coordinate independent, everything in
closed form.

. . .

What if we could *turn one into the other* — with a map we can run **both ways**?

## One Invertible Map, Both Directions

$$\underbrace{z = T(x)}_{\text{forward: simplify}}
\qquad
\underbrace{x = T^{-1}(z)}_{\text{backward: generate}}$$

- **Forward** → Gaussianize: the distortion needed *is* the dependence
  (measure / remove)
- **Backward** → sample a Gaussian, invert: **generate** real scenarios
  (propagate)

. . .

*The same machine powers Modules 1, 3, and 4.*

## Change of Variables · Conserve the Mass

A map can **move and stretch** probability mass — it can't create or destroy it.
The mass in a thin slab is the same on both sides:

$$p_X(x)\,\Delta x \;=\; p_Z(z)\,\Delta z$$

::: {#2e717088 .cell fig-height='2.6' fig-width='10.5' execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=2043 height=502}
:::
:::


**Density = mass ÷ width** — stretch the slab and the density must drop.

## Change of Variables · The Jacobian Is the Stretch

Take the limit — the width ratio becomes the derivative, and in $d$ dimensions the
local **volume** change is the Jacobian determinant:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{1-D:}\quad & p_X(x) = p_Z\big(T(x)\big)\,\big|T'(x)\big| \\[2pt]
d\text{-dim:}\quad & p_X(x) = p_Z\big(T(x)\big)\,\Big|\det \tfrac{\partial T}{\partial x}\Big|
\end{aligned}$$

. . .

- **Forward** — the distortion needed to flatten the data *is* the dependence
  (measure / remove).
- **Backward** — a sampling recipe: draw $z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, apply $T^{-1}$
  (generate).

---

## #1 The 1-D Move: Rank → Gaussian

$$T(x) = \Phi^{-1}\big(\hat F(x)\big)$$

Empirical CDF (→ uniform), then inverse Gaussian CDF. Monotone ⇒ invertible.

::: {#bde56c9e .cell fig-height='3' fig-width='10' execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1972 height=543}
:::
:::


It reshapes one marginal — but can't touch dependence *between* variables.

## #2 RBIG · Why Gaussian Marginals Aren't Enough

The 1-D move fixes one axis at a time. Apply it to **both** axes of a V:

::: {#04551639 .cell fig-height='3' fig-width='10' execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1943 height=542}
:::
:::


Both marginals are now exactly Gaussian — yet the joint is **still a V**: the
dependence lives *between* the axes, beyond any per-axis map.

## #2 RBIG · Rotate, Re-Gaussianize, Repeat

Rotation mixes the axes, so leftover dependence resurfaces *as* non-Gaussian
marginals — which the 1-D move can then flatten. Alternate the two:

::: {#fb2a538b .cell fig-height='3' fig-width='12' execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=2343 height=541}
:::
:::


Loop until the cloud is round — **that alternation, not marginals alone, is RBIG.**

## #2 Forward to Gaussian, Backward to Data

::: {#21b82eb9 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=2144 height=663}
:::
:::


**What it removes going forward, it regenerates going backward.**

## #3 Total Correlation · Make a Meatball

Same ingredients, laid out loose, fill the whole bowl. Bind them into one ball and
they **overlap** — the room you save is exactly what they *share*.

::: {#37c39a88 .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='9.5' execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=1382 height=584}
:::
:::


Same marginals both sides — only the binding differs.

## #3 The Saved Room *Is* Total Correlation

That saved room — every marginal's spread minus the joint's — has a name:

$$\mathrm{TC}(x) = \sum_i H(x_i) - H(x) = \operatorname{KL}\!\big(p \,\|\, \textstyle\prod_i p_i\big)$$

. . .

Gaussianize and you can squeeze it out — and *measure* it — even in high dimensions.

## #3 From Bits Back to ρ

Two variables ⇒ total correlation **is** mutual information — and for a Gaussian
it's a clean function of ρ:

::: {#79824814 .cell fig-height='2.8' fig-width='9' execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](02-gaussianization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1716 height=505}
:::
:::


Linfoot, $R=\sqrt{1-e^{-2I}}$, puts those nats back on the correlation scale —
so MI sits beside Pearson, dCor and HSIC on the scorecard.

## #4 Normalizing Flows — Learn the Map {.center}

RBIG's map is *fixed* (rank-Gaussianize + rotate).

. . .

A **flow** *learns* $T$: a chain of invertible layers, trained by maximum
likelihood — bending to dependence too rich for fixed rotations.

. . .

Same forward/backward spine, more capacity, more training cost
([gauss_flows](https://github.com/jejjohnson/gauss_flows), JAX).

## The Punchline → Demo {.center}

One invertible map, three jobs:

. . .

- **measure** dependence — run it *forward*; what it removes is the answer
- **remove** it — the same measure, as a training penalty *(Module 4)*
- **generate** it — run it *backward*; sample the ball, invert *(Module 3)*

. . .

**The demo:** RBIG and a flow on real returns — estimate the mutual
information, then sample scenarios that keep the co-crash.

. . .

*Next: run it backward as a risk engine — [Uncertainty](03-uncertainty.qmd).*
